body:
You are drafting spoken lines for a video game. Reply with plain text only, in the exact row format given at the end of this message. Do not send messages to anyone else and do not ask questions: decide. Write nothing but the rows (no title, no notes, no Markdown).

THE GAME. "The Crooked Moon" is a single-player, turn-based tactical party RPG built from a folk-horror Dungeons and Dragons campaign. It is set in Wickermoor Hollow, a haunted valley in Druskenvald, a land of endless night under a giant Crooked Moon with a crone's face. The look is a Halloween that never ends, drawn like an 1980s cartoon. A ghost train, the Ghostlight Express, has crashed in the valley; the party is stranded in the Hollow and its village, Wickermoor. The tone is warm, wry and funny on the surface, with real dread and real grief underneath. The player controls a party of four chosen from six companions: Rook Coldwake, Tobin Hayward, Silas Vane, Delphine Ravelle, Lucan Houndstooth and Cordelia Skein. They are quirky, capable adults.

THE NARRATOR. A NARRATOR row is spoken by the Vagrant, the green-skinned ferryman of the ghost train, who tells the tale in a folksy Southern drawl. At the camp fire he is warm and wry, and when a talk turns sad his humour leaves and he goes plain and level. He speaks to the party as "you" and about the companion in the third person, by first name. Present tense, one or two sentences, under about 32 words. Concrete senses (a smell, a sound, a touch, what the hands are doing) over adjectives. Never tell the player what to feel. Never "suddenly". No facts the party could not see. Drop the final g ("hangin'") in about one Narrator row in four, and use no other dialect spelling. He is kind, never mocks a stumble and never makes light of the dead.

RULES FOR EVERY LINE.
1. The companion's voice sheet below comes first. Match its accent, pace, vocabulary and contractions, and the existing lines. Use a pet phrase at most twice in the whole reply and never twice in one talk. Never repeat or closely paraphrase a line already in the voice sheet or the note.
2. A SAY row is the companion speaking: one or two short sentences, under about 28 words. Never put three sentences in one row; start another row instead.
3. The party's options (OPTION rows) are under 12 words, in the plain voice of the party, work at any hour and in any weather, never name a hero, and are never rolls or checks. A reply must always answer the option it follows.
4. Canon limits. Use only the facts in the voice sheet and the note below. Do not invent a new named person, place, monster, event, object the companion carries, or piece of the companion's history. You may invent small, harmless habits, fondnesses, superstitions and turns of phrase, and the look of the fire and the night. Name no place that the note does not name. Never state a dark secret. You may come close to one and step back.
5. Nothing here is a game system: no dice, no checks, no points, no levels, no HP, no "approval", no menus talked about aloud. Plain punctuation only (commas, full stops, hyphens, apostrophes, question marks, quotation marks inside a line when someone is quoted). No em dashes, no semicolons, no brackets, no asterisks, no stage directions, no placeholders.
6. Humour comes from the character, never explained. The sad turn is plain and short.
7. Our own words. Nothing quoted from any book.

THIS REQUEST. Four camp talks about Tobin's personal story, the Thread of Rejuvenation. The companion is TOBIN HAYWARD (call them Tobin in NARRATOR rows). The attached note is the voice sheet and the fact sheet; it describes an older plan for the Thread's beats in places, so take people, objects, manner and background from it, but where it disagrees with THE FIXED FACTS in this brief, the fixed facts win.

HOW A CAMP TALK WORKS. After a rest the player can walk up to a companion who has asked for a word at the fire. It is private, short and warm. The companion speaks first (NARRATOR and SAY rows), the player chooses what the party says from three short options (or two where the talk says so), and the companion answers in their own voice (a REPLY). Then the talk ends. Nothing in it is a roll or a failure, and every reply must leave the talk finished and the fire going: a cool reply is still an ending, never a slammed door. Each reply also carries a REASON row: one sentence beginning "You", past tense, under 14 words, saying what the party did or said as the companion would remember it (for example "You heard me out at the fire" or "You waved it off and went to bed"). A REASON is plain notice text and is not spoken.

THE FIXED FACTS (the beats in the game's journal; the talks tell these, in Tobin's own words, and go no further than they do).
- Tobin's Thread: Tobin's Rejuvenation. What Tobin wants: Find where the Hollow's soil went sick, and make it grow again.
- The Connection already happened in Wickermoor, with Sister Rain. The journal says: "Sister Rain put a seed in Tobin's hand and asked for nothing for it."
- The Discovery, "The Root of the Rot", happens in Skitterdeep (the mine). The journal's line for it: "Under Skitterdeep Tobin tasted where the Hollow's sickness drinks from, and knew it could be cut."
- The Confrontation, "Green from Ash", happens in Hartsblight (the forest). The journal's line for it: "In Hartsblight Tobin faced the fire he never talks about, and the forest grew back where it fell."
Each talk is had at camp AFTER its chapter is over, so Tobin looks back on what happened. You may name Skitterdeep (the mine) in the Discovery and Hartsblight (the forest) in the Confrontation and no other place. Do not describe fights, bosses or villains; Tobin speaks of what was found, felt or chosen.

THE INCITEMENT AS IT PLAYED (for the first talk). Tobin sometimes misses this scene because Tobin is not with the party when it plays in the Conservatory of the Crooked House. Then Tobin goes back alone, and at camp tells the party what was found. These are the facts of the scene; do not change them, you may add small sensory detail:
[rejuvenation_start]
  NARRATOR: Rain drums hard on the glass roof while Tobin steps past the dead vines and presses a burlap thumb to the weeping bark of the bergamot. He jerks it back as if the sap had scalded him.
  TOBIN: Bark's cold, nothing burning here, only a deep sour canker running down the taproot toward that centipede hill.
  NARRATOR: A smell of scorchin' apple-wood fills the damp air, and the mice in his lapels squeak and dive for his pockets. He pulls three straws from his ribs, twists a splint round a cracked twig, and clears his throat hard.
  TOBIN: Cracked clean through the heartwood, and weeping. The rot in this is old, and it runs a long way from here.
  the party can say: What did that tree just show you?
  the party can say: Your hand shook. Did the sap burn you?
  the party can say: Leave the tree. We have a manor to clear.
[rejuvenation_asked]
  NARRATOR: Tobin draws his stiff pruning knife and tests the flat of the blade against his burlap thumb, steadying his grip.
  TOBIN: Blight doesn't stop at the fence line when the rootstock is sour. We track that seam down the valley and tie off the rot.
[rejuvenation_admitted]
  NARRATOR: He tucks the loose straw back between his ribs and strokes a trembling mouse through the cloth of his pocket.
  TOBIN: Sap's cold as well-water. Just a whiff of old orchard smoke in the grain. I've known a bad fire in my time, and it doesn't bear dwelling on.
[rejuvenation_moved_on]
  NARRATOR: Tobin folds his pruning knife shut with a dry click, slides it into his coat, and dusts the damp bark from his knuckles.
  TOBIN: Right, the splint will hold the bough till morning. Keep your boots off the surface roots as we go.

THE TALKS. Write these four talks, in this order, with these keys.

TALK incitement. Tobin tells the party about the Conservatory of the Crooked House as one short story at the fire. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 3 or 4 SAY rows (the story, in their own words, ending on a plain statement of how it left them). TWO options only: OPTION 1 asks to hear more or says something that shares the moment; OPTION 2 is the quiet way on, leaving Tobin to it. Two replies of 1 NARRATOR row (optional) and 1 or 2 SAY rows. No REASON rows in this talk.

TALK discovery. Tobin has come back from Skitterdeep (the mine) with the Discovery, and wants to tell it. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row to open the scene at the fire, then 6 to 8 SAY rows (one more NARRATOR row is allowed in the middle) that tell what the journal line says in Tobin's own words and end on the turn: how it sits with them, with one thing left unsaid (never the dark secret: no names, deeds or places from the note's dark-secret section). Three options: OPTION 1 asks Tobin to say more; OPTION 2 is the answer most like what Tobin would want to hear, meeting Tobin on Tobin's own terms; OPTION 3 is the quiet way on, civil but brisk, brushing it past. Three replies of 1 to 3 rows each, each ending the talk, each with a REASON row. The cool reply (3) must still leave the Discovery told.

TALK confrontation_wait. Tobin is at their lowest regard for the party (Strained), and has the Confrontation to tell about Hartsblight (the forest) but is holding it back until things are mended. This talk is short. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row and 3 or 4 SAY rows: Tobin says there is something to say about it and it will keep, and says, in Tobin's own voice, what matters to Tobin and that the party's way has drifted from it (do not claim any specific deed the party did). Three options: OPTION 1 listens and owns it (the way to mend); OPTION 2 answers coldly; OPTION 3 says nothing and gives Tobin room (its option text is plain words such as "Say nothing. Stay by the fire."; this reply has NO REASON row). Replies of 1 or 2 rows. Nothing is lost for good: even the cold reply leaves the door open.

TALK confrontation. Tobin's story comes to a head. Opening: 1 NARRATOR row, then 7 to 9 SAY rows (one more NARRATOR row allowed in the middle) that tell what the journal line says in Tobin's own words: the heart of their act-three story, plain and a little raw, never grand; Tobin may say that something from before has found them, but must NOT name or describe the person, the act or the event behind the dark secret (no names, deeds, places or objects from the note's dark-secret section, or from its Climax and Catharsis sections): say only what it was like to stand one's ground against it; end on the turn and a question or a long silence. Three options: OPTION 1 asks Tobin to say more; OPTION 2 is the answer most like what Tobin needs to hear; OPTION 3 is the quiet way on, brushing it past. Three replies of 1 to 3 rows each, each ending the talk, each with a REASON row. The cool reply must still leave the Confrontation told.

THE ROW FORMAT (exact). One row per line, rows in this order, nothing else:

TALK <key>
NARRATOR: <line>
SAY: <line>
SAY: <line>
OPTION 1: <what the party says>
OPTION 2: <what the party says>
OPTION 3: <what the party says>
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: <optional line>
SAY: <line>
REASON: You <what the party did>
REPLY 2
...
REPLY 3
...

TALK <key> starts a talk (the keys are given below, exactly). The rows before the first OPTION are the talk's opening. Each REPLY block holds one optional NARRATOR row first, then one or two SAY rows, then a REASON row (and an INSPIRE row where the talk asks for one). Write exactly the talks listed, in the order listed, with the row counts given.

The TALK keys, exactly: incitement, discovery, confrontation_wait, confrontation.

ATTACHED DOCUMENTS. Two documents come attached to this message; read both before you write. `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/tobin_hayward-voice-and-beats.md` holds the voice sheet for TOBIN HAYWARD (age, accent, pace, pet phrases, existing lines) and the character file (what Tobin likes and dislikes, the Thread, the dark secret you must never state). `tasks/crooked-moon-companions/tobin_hayward-camp-talks.md` holds the camp talks already written for Tobin, as voice examples: do not repeat their topics or lines.
result:
TALK incitement
NARRATOR: Tobin sits three paces back from the fire, wipin' green sap from his pruning knife with a twist of dry straw.
SAY: I stepped back into that broken glasshouse while the rain came down, just to take the measure of the bergamot tree.
SAY: One thumb on the weeping bark and my whole arm went cold, because a sour black canker is eating straight through the heartwood.
SAY: Worse, the sap carried a phantom reek of scorching apple-wood that had the mice diving for my pockets.
SAY: I splinted the cracked twig with three straws from my ribs, though it left my fingers shaking in my cuffs.
OPTION 1: Where does that rot run to, and why did the smoke shake you?
OPTION 2: The splint will hold for tonight. Get some rest.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: He clicks the pruning knife shut and presses two burlap fingers against his pocket until the rustling inside settles.
SAY: The seam runs down the taproot toward the hills, and we can track it and cut it clean.
SAY: As for the smoke, a straw man has no business near an orchard fire, and old ash is best left in the ground.
REPLY 2
NARRATOR: Tobin slides the folded knife into his duster and brushes a flake of damp bark from his knee.
SAY: Aye, the binding is tight enough to see the bough through till morning.
SAY: Keep your boots off the surface roots when we march, and I will keep my eye on the soil.
TALK discovery
NARRATOR: Tobin squats on an upturned crate well clear of the sparks, scraping grey webbing off his boot heel with a dry twig.
SAY: Down under Skitterdeep, where the stone sweats, I pinched a flake of peeling birch bark onto my tongue to read the vintage.
SAY: That mine wasn't the beginning of the parish sickness, only a cellar where the rot pooled and fed.
SAY: I tasted the cold vein where the Hollow's blight drinks from, running under the rock like a poisoned ditch.
NARRATOR: He spits into the dark grass beside his boot and wipes his stitched mouth with the back of his wrist.
SAY: A deep taproot, sour as dead turnip, and it reaches all the way into the timber up the ridge.
SAY: Still, any root that drinks can be severed if the surgeon has a steady blade.
SAY: Sister Rain gave me a clean seed in Wickermoor for nothing, and I mean to find it an honest row.
SAY: Only, tasting that black water brought back a dry summer I thought I had stitched shut for good.
OPTION 1: What kind of summer leaves a taste like that behind?
OPTION 2: If the root can be cut, we bring a sharp blade and clear the row.
OPTION 3: Keep the map in your head. We move at first light.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: Tobin pulls his hat low over his stitched brow and touches the front seam of his coat with a flat thumb.
SAY: A season where the blight moved faster than the pruning hook, and a man made a foul ledger of his neighbours' trees.
SAY: That account is closed, and I will not balance this valley's books with a torch.
REASON: You asked what kind of summer left that taste behind.
REPLY 2
NARRATOR: A faint papery rustle comes from his chest as he straightens his lapels and nods once.
SAY: Now that is sound husbandry, plain and brisk.
SAY: Good soil, bad seed, and a clean cut at the taproot before the whole acre goes sour.
REASON: You agreed to cut the root clean and clear the row.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: He tucks the scrap of twig into his herb satchel and buckles the flap down tight.
SAY: The seam is marked in my ledger, never fret.
SAY: Give me ten minutes to check the mice for mine-damp and I am ready for the road.
REASON: You told me to keep the map in my head and get ready to march.
TALK confrontation_wait
NARRATOR: Tobin stands by the baggage cart with his arms crossed, his turnip-lantern hanging cold against his wooden collarbone.
SAY: There is an account from Hartsblight sitting in my chest, and it will stay there until our seams are straighter.
SAY: We are meant to be surgeons in this valley, scraping out the canker and saving what can still grow.
SAY: Lately your boots have been heavy on the living roots and careless with the sparks.
SAY: I do not open my private ledger to folk who treat a sick parish like kindling.
OPTION 1: You're right. We've been careless, and we'll mind the living ground.
OPTION 2: Keep your stories to yourself, then, so long as you do your work.
OPTION 3: Say nothing. Stay by the fire.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: He lets out a dry, reedy breath and adjusts the pale primrose sproutin' from his left cuff.
SAY: Words are cheap twine, friend, so let me see how you walk the rows tomorrow.
SAY: Keep the sparks off the good timber and we will speak of the forest when the camp is quiet.
REASON: You owned your careless steps and promised to mind the living ground.
REPLY 2
NARRATOR: Tobin's stitched mouth pulls into a flat line, and he turns his shoulder toward the dark trees.
SAY: My blade is sharp and my bindings hold, you will have no complaint on that score.
SAY: Just keep your lantern three paces off my back while we march.
REASON: You told me to keep my stories to myself and just do the work.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: Tobin watches the coals settle for a long two-beat count, then taps the brim of his hat and steps back into the dark.
SAY: Mind the damp in your bedroll.
TALK confrontation
NARRATOR: Tobin sits on a dry log with his elbows on his knees, turnin' a clean bit of ash bark over in his burlap hands.
SAY: Up in Hartsblight, when the grey dust settled, the ancient timber answered my thumb without a drop of poison in the sap.
SAY: Only the wood did not show me mushroom or stag-rot.
SAY: It caught the memory right out of my own ribs, hot cinder-smoke and a blazing roof I never speak of.
SAY: In my mortal seasons, when a black canker took the rows, I chose the torch over the pruning knife, and I woke in this valley made of dry straw.
NARRATOR: His breath shortens, crowding the words together, and he presses a flat palm hard against the middle of his chest.
SAY: Every spark since has had me stepping three paces back, terrified my own hands would turn a curable blight into an ash-heap twice.
SAY: In Hartsblight I stood my ground against that heat and tied the split bark instead of running or striking a match.
SAY: Clean green shoots broke straight through the char before we left the trees.
SAY: Do you reckon one clean row pays a speck toward an acre a man ruined with his own hand?
OPTION 1: Tell me what happened when you stood your ground in the smoke.
OPTION 2: It doesn't erase the old ledger, Tobin, but the new green is real.
OPTION 3: The forest is growing back. Leave the old ash behind.
REPLY 1
NARRATOR: The Vagrant sets his tin cup down without a sound while Tobin steadies his breathing and lets his hand drop from his chest.
SAY: My wrists smoked in the memory of it, and every mouse in my coat went still as stone.
SAY: I kept my thumb on the living grain until the phantom fire starved for fuel, and the sap ran sweet again.
REASON: You asked what it took to stand my ground in the smoke.
REPLY 2
NARRATOR: Tobin looks down at the pale primrose on his cuff, then gives a crisp, single nod.
SAY: Aye, a surgeon does not un-scar the bark, he only sees the next season gets its water.
SAY: Hold still a second, you're fraying at the hem and I have a spare length of good twine.
REASON: You told me the old ledger stays, but the new green is real.
REPLY 3
NARRATOR: Tobin tucks the flake of clean ash bark into his waistcoat pocket and dusts his palms together.
SAY: Plain enough, and no sense letting the dew rust the shears while we stare at yesterday.
SAY: The timber in Hartsblight will hold its own rows now, and so will I.
REASON: You told me the forest is growing back and to leave the old ash behind.
